When the editor of the world’s most prestigious medical journal concluded that much of the clinical research it published could no longer be trusted, the problem was no longer abstract.
Marcia Angell, a pathologist who joined the New England Journal of Medicine staff in 1979, rose to executive editor and then served as interim editor-in-chief from 1999 to June 2000. She stepped down after more than two decades at the journal, formally to write a book. The deeper context was her growing conviction, formed from years of editing manuscripts, that pharmaceutical industry influence had compromised the independence of clinical research. She and previous editors had enforced strict conflict-of-interest rules, yet industry-sponsored studies continued to arrive with designs, analyses, and selective reporting that favored the sponsor’s product. Negative results were often suppressed, side effects minimized, and “academic” authors frequently carried undisclosed financial ties. 
In a widely cited 2009 New York Review of Books essay, Angell wrote the line that crystallized her position: “It is simply no longer possible to believe much of the clinical research that is published, or to rely on the judgment of trusted physicians or authoritative medical guidelines. I take no pleasure in this conclusion, which I reached slowly and reluctantly over my two decades as an editor of The New England Journal of Medicine.” She described an industry that had shifted from discovering useful drugs toward marketing, co-opting academic medical centers, researchers, and even the journals that were supposed to serve as independent arbiters. Her 2000 editorial “Is Academic Medicine for Sale?” and later book The Truth About the Drug Companies expanded the critique, arguing that commercial priorities systematically distorted what research was done, how it was conducted, and what reached publication. 
Angell’s departure marked the end of an era of tighter editorial resistance to industry influence at the NEJM. Her public statements afterward made clear that she viewed the problem as systemic rather than isolated: once the bulk of clinical research depended on commercial funding, journals could no longer function as reliable filters of medical evidence.

hits.name: Dr Shawn Baker 🥩
hits.text:
Doctors still slice into arthritic knees, scrape the cartilage, and flush out the joint hundreds of thousands of times a year—even though a major study proved the real surgery works no better than fake surgery.

In 2002, surgeon J. Bruce Moseley and his team published a carefully designed study in the New England Journal of Medicine. They took 180 patients with painful knee osteoarthritis who had already tried medicines and other treatments. The patients were randomly split into three groups. One group got the full arthroscopic surgery: the doctor washed out the knee with a lot of fluid, shaved rough cartilage, and trimmed any torn or worn pieces of the meniscus (the soft cushion in the knee). A second group got only the washing (lavage). The third group got a sham, or fake, surgery. Those patients were sedated, the surgeon made the same small skin cuts, and the operating room team made the sounds and motions of real surgery—but nothing ever went inside the joint.
Neither the patients nor the people checking their results knew who got the real surgery and who got the fake one. For two full years, researchers tracked pain and how well people could walk and climb stairs. At every check-up, the three groups looked the same. The real operations did not reduce pain or improve function any better than the pretend surgery. The confidence intervals even ruled out any meaningful difference. Patients in all groups felt a bit better, which the researchers attributed to the placebo effect—the power of believing you had a real treatment—plus the natural ups and downs of the condition.
At the time of the study, more than 650,000 of these arthroscopic procedures were already being done each year in the United States. Rates of pure “clean-out” surgeries for osteoarthritis later fell somewhat after guidelines advised against them, yet knee arthroscopy (especially for degenerative meniscus tears that often occur alongside arthritis) remains extremely common. Recent data still show hundreds of thousands of knee arthroscopies performed annually in the U.S. alone. The Moseley trial and later similar studies continue to show that, for typical age-related knee wear, the mechanical work inside the joint adds little or nothing beyond the placebo effect and standard non-surgical care.
hits.draft_en:
Dr Shawn Baker points to a 2002 New England Journal of Medicine study on arthritic knees. Surgeons were cleaning out the joint hundreds of thousands of times a year — washing, scraping cartilage, trimming the meniscus — even though a careful trial found the real surgery worked no better than fake surgery.

180 patients, three groups: full clean-out, wash-only, or sham cuts with nothing done inside. For two years the pain and walking scores looked the same. Placebo and the natural ups and downs of the condition did as much as the knife.

Rates of pure clean-out ops fell after guidelines changed, but knee arthroscopy for age-related wear is still common. Worth a second opinion before you let someone scrape a worn knee that might calm down with physio and time.

Eating blueberries improves vascular function.

One cup per day is effective, but half a cup does not not produce the same benefit.

Adults with metabolic syndrome that ate one cup rather than only a half-cup or matched placebo improved flow-mediated dilation (FMD) by about 1.5 percentage points in a six-month randomized trial.

FMD measures how effectively an artery widens when blood flow increases, essentially a "stress test" for the endothelium. It's relevant because studies have shown it is a strong predictor of future cardiovascular disease events.

The one-cup dose is consistent with other studies showing cardiovascular, metabolic, and brain-health benefits of blueberries.
hits.draft_en:
Dr Rhonda Patrick says eating blueberries improves how your blood vessels work.

One cup a day helped adults with metabolic syndrome. Half a cup didn't do the same job. In a six-month trial, the one-cup group improved flow-mediated dilation by about 1.5 percentage points — that's how well an artery widens when blood flow rises, and it's a predictor of future heart trouble.

Same one-cup dose lines up with other studies on heart, metabolism and brain.

Plain takeaway: a cup of blueberries is a cheap add-on at smoko if your vessels and metabolic numbers need a nudge.

hits.name: Dr Shawn Baker 🥩
hits.text:
For nearly two million years, the dominant story of human evolution wasn’t one of flexible omnivores cleverly mixing plants and animals. It was the rise of specialized hypercarnivorous apex predators whose bodies, genes, and behavior were built around hunting large, fat-rich animals—and whose biology still carries that signature today.
In their 2021 paper “The Evolution of the Human Trophic Level During the Pleistocene” (American Journal of Physical Anthropology), Miki Ben-Dor, Raphaël Sirtoli, and Ran Barkai reconstruct what humans actually ate during the Pleistocene without relying on the usual ethnographic analogies to recent hunter-gatherers (whose environments and prey bases were radically different). 
They assembled 25 independent lines of evidence drawn from human physiology and genetics, archaeology, paleontology, and zoology. The cumulative picture is clear: the Homo lineage shifted from a lower trophic level toward a high, carnivorous position beginning with Homo habilis, peaking with Homo erectus, and remaining elevated for most of the Pleistocene. Humans functioned as social hunters of large prey (megafauna and large mammals) and, by comparison with modern social carnivores, as hypercarnivores deriving roughly 70% or more of their calories from animal sources. 
Key categories of evidence include:
•  Physiology and metabolism: Human stomach acidity is unusually high—even compared with other predators—consistent with consuming meat that could sit for days (as from large kills). Genetic patterns show adaptations favoring a fat-rich animal diet in humans while chimpanzees show the opposite shift toward sugars.
•  Archaeology and stable isotopes: Multiple stable-isotope studies of prehistoric human remains indicate high animal-protein diets until late in the Paleolithic. Zooarchaeology shows repeated targeting of large herbivores, with early access to high-ranking prey.
•  Paleontology and ecology: Humans entered and competed within the large-predator guild; prey-size decline later tracked changes in human morphology, technology, and diet. Large animals provided the fat and caloric density that smaller, leaner prey could not match efficiently.
•  Zoological analogy: Social carnivores that hunt large prey are hypercarnivores; the human pattern of large-prey specialization aligns with this category.
A reversal toward lower trophic levels appears in the Upper Paleolithic, strengthens in the Mesolithic/Epipaleolithic and Neolithic, and culminates with agriculture. The authors emphasize that modern human genetics, metabolism, and morphology still retain “the memory of an adaptation to a trophic level” that was predominantly carnivorous for the great majority of the Pleistocene. 
This multidisciplinary approach—twenty-five convergent lines rather than a single analogy—offers one of the more robust reconstructions of ancestral human diet available. It reframes the long Pleistocene as a period of specialized large-game hunting rather than generalized omnivory, with downstream implications for understanding human brain expansion, morphology, and the later dietary transition driven by declining megafauna.

hits.name: Dr Shawn Baker 🥩
hits.text:
Imagine walking into an emergency room with a broken arm. You leave with a bill so high it looks like a phone number. Here’s the surprising part: your insurance company can actually make more money when that bill gets bigger.
The Affordable Care Act (ACA) created a rule called the Medical Loss Ratio. It says insurance companies must spend at least 80% of the money you pay them (your premiums) on actual medical care. They can keep only 15–20% for running the company and for profit. The goal was to stop insurers from pocketing too much of your money.
But there’s a catch. The rule limits profit as a percentage, not as a fixed dollar amount. When medical costs rise, insurance companies raise premiums. The percentage they keep stays the same, but the actual dollars they keep grow.
Here’s a simple example. Say an insurance company collects $100 in premiums. It spends $85 on medical care and keeps $15. Now medical costs rise 20%. The company charges $120 in premiums, spends $102 on care, and keeps $18. Same percentage—but more money in their pocket. The more expensive healthcare becomes, the bigger their profit can get, without them doing anything differently.
This reduces the pressure on insurance companies to fight hard against rising prices. Higher bills from hospitals and doctors simply expand the pie they get a slice of.
Some large insurance companies have also bought hospitals, clinics, and pharmacies. They can pay their own businesses higher prices. Those payments count as “medical spending” under the rule, helping them meet the percentage requirement, while the extra money stays inside the company.
The rule was meant to protect patients. Instead, it can reward a system where higher costs mean higher absolute profits for insurers. That’s one reason medical bills keep climbing while insurance companies stay profitable.

According to the EPIC-Oxford study, the top two major causes of death among vegans are cancer and heart disease.
The European Prospective Investigation into Cancer and Nutrition–Oxford (EPIC-Oxford) is one of the largest long-term cohort studies examining diet and health in the UK. 

A key 2016 analysis (Appleby et al., American Journal of Clinical Nutrition) pooled data from EPIC-Oxford and the Oxford Vegetarian Study, tracking more than 60,000 participants—including roughly 2,228 vegans—over more than a million person-years of follow-up. 

There were 5,294 deaths before age 90.
Among the 166 deaths recorded in the vegan group, cancer (malignant neoplasms) and circulatory/heart disease were the leading causes by absolute numbers. This mirrors patterns seen across the other diet groups and in the broader UK population. When researchers compared vegans directly with regular meat-eaters, there were no statistically significant differences in mortality from malignant cancer, circulatory disease, ischemic heart disease, cerebrovascular disease, or respiratory disease. 

Hazard ratios for these outcomes generally ranged from about 0.8 to 1.5, but confidence intervals were wide because of the relatively small number of vegan deaths.
All-cause mortality was also similar across diet groups. Vegans had a hazard ratio of 1.14 (95% CI 0.97–1.35) compared with regular meat-eaters—not a significant difference.

Dr Shawn Baker cites the EPIC-Oxford study: among vegans in that UK cohort, the top two causes of death by raw count were cancer and heart disease — same as the wider population.

So the headline "vegans die of cancer and heart disease" is true as a count, and also true of everyone else. The study doesn't prove vegan diets are safer or more dangerous on those endpoints. Don't let a chart cherry-pick your lunch.

In 1931, British researchers measured two neighboring Kenyan tribes living side by side—and found that the cattle-herding pastoralists stood five inches taller, weighed 23 pounds more, and were 50% stronger than their farming neighbors.

Gilks compared the Maasai, whose traditional diet centered on milk, meat, and blood from their cattle, with the Kikuyu, whose diet was built mainly on maize, millet, sweet potatoes, and other plant foods. What if the “heart-healthy” low-fat, low-cholesterol diet that doctors have pushed for decades doesn’t just lower your LDL—it also makes you more likely to snap, slap, bite, or lash out?
That’s exactly what a series of controlled experiments on cynomolgus macaques (Macaca fascicularis) demonstrated in the 1990s. Jay R. Kaplan and colleagues housed groups of these highly social monkeys and fed them either high-fat, high-cholesterol diets or the kind of lower-fat, lower-cholesterol “prudent” diets recommended by the American Heart Association. Across multiple studies, the animals on the low-cholesterol regimens consistently showed more contact aggression—slapping, grabbing, grappling, and biting—along with more submissive displays and less affiliative behavior such as sitting in passive body contact or staying close to one another.
In one key experiment, juvenile monkeys eating a low-cholesterol diet were more aggressive and less social than their high-cholesterol counterparts; they also had lower levels of the serotonin metabolite 5-HIAA in their cerebrospinal fluid. Another within-subjects design switched animals from a very high-fat diet to a low-fat one and observed the same pattern: aggression rose while affiliation and proximity fell. Body weight stayed comparable, isolating the effect to the dietary cholesterol and fat change itself.
The proposed mechanism runs through serotonin. Low central serotonergic activity is one of the most reliable biological correlates of impulsivity and aggression across species. Cholesterol is a major component of neuronal membranes; reducing it appears to impair serotonin receptor function or signaling in brain regions that normally dampen impulsive and violent behavior. The result is a weaker “brake” on aggression.
These primate findings line up with human observations linking naturally low or medically lowered cholesterol to higher rates of suicide, accidents, and violence-related deaths. While the monkey data are experimental and the human data largely correlational, together they suggest that pushing cholesterol very low may carry behavioral costs for at least some individuals—costs that rarely make it into the standard public-health script about diet and heart disease.

Charles Washington is a foundational figure in the modern zero-carb (all-meat/carnivore) movement and the founder of Zeroing In On Health (ZIOH). 
In early 2007, Washington was obese (around 221 pounds), pre-diabetic, and facing potential medication. He first tried a low-fat, portion-controlled plan, then shifted to carbohydrate restriction after discovering low-carb approaches via writers like Gary Taubes and accounts of clinicians such as Dr. Mary Vernon. He began Atkins Induction but never “climbed the carb ladder.” By August 2007 he eliminated all plant foods entirely, adopting a zero-carb regimen of meat and water. He lost roughly 78 pounds, normalized blood pressure and lipids, and reported broad improvements in skin, energy, strength, libido, and overall well-being. 
He became an active runner (including marathons and high weekly mileage) while eating primarily commercial supermarket meats—beef, pork, and chicken—typically around 2–4 pounds daily, drinking water, and using salt or spices only sparingly. His philosophy treats meat and water as the non-negotiable foundation; other animal foods (eggs, occasional dairy) are secondary, and plant foods are excluded as “food.” He has long maintained that a properly adapted woman can carry a healthy pregnancy on zero-carb, a view that drew sharp criticism from low-carb authorities of the era but has since been supported by community experience. 
As a moderator on Jimmy Moore’s Atkins forum, Washington took over a nearly empty Zero Carb thread. It grew so dominant that the group was effectively pushed out. In October 2008 he founded Zeroing In On Health as a dedicated space where zero plant foods was the default rather than a fringe exception. The group (later a major Facebook community) has provided practical support, guidelines rooted in long-term practitioners (including Owsley “the Bear” Stanley), and peer counsel to thousands. Washington has worked for the U.S. Army Corps of Engineers and has remained a consistent, low-key mentor in the zero-carb/carnivore world for nearly two decades, emphasizing simplicity, eating to satiety, and the idea that a healthy body enables exercise rather than the reverse. 
His early advocacy helped establish the practical, community-driven wing of the all-meat dietary approach that later expanded into the broader carnivore movement.

Vioxx (rofecoxib), a COX-2 selective painkiller launched by Merck in 1999, became one of the biggest drug-safety scandals of the modern era. Marketed as an arthritis and pain treatment with fewer gastrointestinal side effects than traditional NSAIDs like naproxen, it quickly became a blockbuster, with annual sales exceeding $2 billion and roughly 20 million Americans (and more than 80 million people worldwide) taking it before its withdrawal. 
Internal Merck documents show the company had indications of cardiovascular risks years earlier. Memos from the mid-to-late 1990s discussed potential increases in thrombotic events linked to the drug’s mechanism. The 2000 VIGOR trial (versus naproxen) revealed a substantially higher rate of heart attacks on Vioxx. On March 9, 2000, Merck research chief Edward Scolnick emailed colleagues that the cardiovascular events “are clearly there,” calling it a “shame” and “mechanism-based as we worried it was.” Public statements at the time often attributed the difference to a protective effect of naproxen or emphasized a favorable profile, while internal discussions considered reformulation ideas and study designs that might minimize unflattering comparisons. Merck disclosed data to the FDA and later added label warnings, but the drug stayed on the market amid aggressive marketing. 
The decisive public evidence came in 2004 from the placebo-controlled APPROVe trial (for colon polyps), which showed roughly double the rate of heart attacks and strokes after about 18 months. Merck voluntarily withdrew Vioxx worldwide on September 30, 2004. Estimates of harm, including a widely cited Lancet analysis, put U.S. excess heart attacks in the tens of thousands (around 88,000 with roughly 38,000 deaths in one model), though figures vary. 
The aftermath featured tens of thousands of lawsuits. Merck, without admitting liability, settled most personal-injury claims for $4.85 billion in 2007 and paid additional sums in regulatory and investor resolutions. The episode highlighted gaps in post-marketing surveillance, the role of marketing in shaping scientific presentation, and the challenge of balancing GI benefits against cardiovascular risks—prompting tighter scrutiny of COX-2 inhibitors and greater emphasis on cardiovascular safety trials for new pain drugs.

Richard Horton, editor-in-chief of The Lancet, concluded that medical journals had “devolved into information-laundering operations for the pharmaceutical industry.” 
This statement comes from his March 2004 New York Review of Books essay “The Dawn of McScience.” He described how companies sponsor meetings, pay speakers, have communications firms turn the talks into articles (often with minimal or no peer review), and then pay publishers large sums to run them as journal supplements. The result, he argued, is marketing dressed up as science that seeds the literature with weaker evidence used to promote products. 
Around the same period, in written and oral evidence to the UK House of Commons Health Select Committee (2004–2005), Horton described the journal–industry relationship as “somewhere between symbiotic and parasitic,” noting that it had swung too far toward the parasitic side. He highlighted financial pressures (e.g., companies promising large reprint orders if a favorable paper is published, or threatening to pull papers if criticism is not softened) and listed roughly 10 distorting practices, including: 
•  Manipulation or selective reporting of findings
•  Bias toward positive results in industry-sponsored studies
•  Hiding negative or adverse data
•  Ghostwriting
•  Lightly peer-reviewed supplements used for marketing
•  Undisclosed conflicts of interest
He stated that commercial sponsorship of research and its intrusion into academia represented “one of the gravest threats to the independent evaluation of new medicines—indeed to the notion of an independent science base,” and that the for-profit motive of the sector clashes with public-health values and independent scientific research. 
In a 2013 Lancet piece (“Falling out with pharma”), Horton withdrew the journal’s support from industry-linked guidance on doctor–pharma collaboration, saying the document’s claims did not match the evidence on company behavior regarding transparency, medical education, and prescribing influence. 
His better-known 2015 editorial (“Offline: What is medicine’s 5 sigma?”) was broader—arguing that “much of the scientific literature, perhaps half, may simply be untrue” due to small samples, invalid analyses, tiny effects, and “flagrant conflicts of interest”—but conflicts of interest (often industry-related) were explicitly part of that critique. 
These statements reflect Horton’s long-standing concerns about industry influence on the medical evidence base rather than a single one-off finding.

What if the real key to living longer isn’t just how strong you are—but how fast you can move that strength? A landmark 2025 study in Mayo Clinic Proceedings shows that muscle power (force times velocity) predicts mortality far more powerfully than traditional strength in middle-aged and older adults. 
Researchers from the CLINIMEX Exercise cohort followed 3,889 adults aged 46–75 (roughly two-thirds men) for a median of nearly 11 years. They measured relative muscle power—how much force someone could produce quickly during an upper-row movement, scaled to body weight—and relative strength via a standard handgrip test. After adjusting for age, body composition, and health conditions, the results were striking: people in the lowest power category faced roughly 6–7 times the mortality risk of those in the highest category (hazard ratios of 5.88 for men and 6.90 for women). Strength showed only weak, nonsignificant links to death. 
In other words, the ability to generate force rapidly mattered more for survival than maximal force alone. Power declines faster with age than pure strength, and it underpins everyday tasks that keep people independent—rising quickly from a chair, climbing stairs, recovering from a stumble, or catching yourself in a fall.
Typical athletic activities and tests that demand power include vertical or broad jumps, medicine-ball throws or slams, power cleans or snatches, sprint starts, plyometric hops, and rapid chair rises or sit-to-stands performed as explosively as possible. Even an upright row or push performed at maximum speed (as used in the study) captures the force-velocity product that pure strength tests miss.
The practical takeaway is clear: training that emphasizes speed and explosiveness—alongside traditional strength work—may offer an underappreciated lever for extending both lifespan and healthspan.

Doctors often give cortisone (steroid) shots straight into painful joints to calm swelling and ease pain. They work well for a short time. But growing research shows these shots may make arthritis worse over the long run, especially when used again and again.
In a careful 2017 study, people with knee arthritis got either a real cortisone shot or a saltwater shot every three months for two years. The cortisone group lost more cartilage—the smooth cushion that protects the bones—than the group that got the fake shot. Pain levels ended up about the same. The researchers said the repeated shots did not help and may have hurt the joint.
A newer 2025 study looked at MRI scans from hundreds of people in a big arthritis project. Those who got one cortisone shot showed more joint damage two years later than people who got no shot or who got a different gel-like injection (hyaluronic acid). The cortisone group had more cartilage breakdown. The other injection seemed to slow the damage.
A review of several studies found that people who received cortisone shots were about twice as likely to show signs of cartilage loss on scans. Some reports also describe rare but serious cases, especially in hips, where a joint collapses faster than expected after a shot.
Not every study agrees. Some long-term checks of real patients found no clear rise in knee replacements after cortisone shots. Still, the pattern is clear enough that many experts now urge caution.
Cortisone calms inflammation fast, but it can also slow the joint’s ability to repair itself. One or two shots for a bad flare may be fine. Frequent shots, though, look riskier for the structure of the joint.
Talk with your doctor about how often to use them, and ask about other options that ease pain without speeding up wear and tear. Your joints have to last a lifetime—treat them carefully.

Imagine a baby orangutan still nursing from its mom at age seven or eight—clinging tight for years while learning to climb and forage. Now picture a human toddler already eating solid foods by age two. That huge difference in weaning time is one of the biggest puzzles in human evolution, and a 2012 study cracked it with a simple idea: eating meat.
Scientists looked at weaning times across 67 different mammals, from rodents to big cats to apes. They built a model that predicted when each species would stop nursing. The biggest factor was brain size—bigger brains take longer to develop, so animals with large brains tend to nurse longer. Body posture and movement also mattered a bit. But diet made a real difference too.
When the model left humans out and tried to predict our weaning time, it got it almost exactly right—about two years and four or five months after birth. That matched the average age from dozens of traditional human societies that don’t use modern formula or early solid foods. Chimpanzees and orangutans, our closest ape relatives, nurse for five to eight years. Humans stop much earlier.
The key difference? Carnivory—eating a significant amount of meat. The study concluded that adding meat to the diet was both necessary and sufficient to explain why humans wean so young. Meat is dense in calories and nutrients, so mothers can support a growing baby’s big brain without needing to nurse for years. Early weaning also lets mothers have babies more often, which helped human populations grow.
In short, the same rules that set weaning times across mammals also apply to us. Our early shift to eating meat didn’t just change what we put on our plates—it reshaped how long our kids stay dependent on milk and helped make human life history unique.

Over the past generation and a half, America has quietly lost nearly half its cattle ranchers.
According to USDA Census of Agriculture data and analyses from producer groups such as R-CALF USA, the country has shed more than 650,000–700,000 beef cattle operations since around 1980. By the 2022 Census, roughly 622,000 operations with at least one beef cow remained—down from levels that were roughly double that figure a generation earlier. One accounting places the drop from about 1.6 million cattle operations in the mid-1980s to roughly 880,000 by 2022, a decline of about 45 percent. The pace has not slowed: between 2017 and 2022 alone, nearly 107,000 beef operations exited, a loss rate exceeding 20,000 per year. 
This is not a story of vanishing demand. Americans still eat large quantities of beef, and total production has been sustained through larger animals, better genetics, improved feed efficiency, and consolidation. What has disappeared are the independent family ranches—especially the smaller and mid-sized ones that once dotted rural landscapes. Most remaining operations are still modest (the majority own fewer than 50 cows), yet the bulk of the national herd is increasingly concentrated in larger herds. The largest operations have grown even as the overall number of ranchers shrinks.
The forces behind the exit are familiar and compounding. Four major packers now control the great majority of beef processing, leaving many ranchers as price-takers in a highly concentrated market. Rising costs for land, feed, labor, equipment, and interest rates have squeezed margins. Prolonged droughts forced herd liquidations. An aging producer base (average age near 58) faces limited succession, while high capital barriers discourage younger entrants. Urban sprawl, regulatory pressures on public lands, and competition from imports have added further pressure.
The result is a quieter countryside: fewer pickup trucks at the sale barn, fewer multi-generational operations passing down knowledge and land, and greater vulnerability in a supply chain that once rested on thousands of independent producers. Rural communities that depended on those ranchers for economic activity and local identity have felt the contraction. While the beef on the plate remains abundant, the people who raise the cattle have become markedly fewer—nearly half of them gone in a span shorter than many living ranchers’ careers.

Imagine skipping every plate of broccoli, every carrot stick, and every salad for your whole life—and still becoming one of the most famous voices in sports while staying active into your 80s. That’s the story of Al Michaels.
Al Michaels is the legendary play-by-play announcer known for calling NFL games, Super Bowls, and the unforgettable “Miracle on Ice” at the 1980 Olympics. For decades he has said the same surprising thing: he has never knowingly eaten a vegetable. 
It started when he was a kid. Born in 1944 to teenage parents, his mother let him eat what he wanted. He pushed the vegetables away and never stopped. As an adult he has stuck to meat, poultry, fish, starches, and dairy. Restaurants he visits know to leave the greens off his plate. He has even joked that he might hold the record for living the longest without eating a vegetable, and that he has “proven that man does not need vegetables to survive.” 
Michaels is now in his early 80s and still working. He continues as the lead voice of Amazon’s Thursday Night Football and shows no signs of slowing down. Friends and colleagues describe him as sharp, prepared, and still excited about big games. While most people are told they must eat vegetables to stay healthy, Michaels has built a long career and active life on a diet that skips them completely.
His story doesn’t prove vegetables are useless for everyone, but it does show that one person can thrive for decades while avoiding them. For Michaels, steak and the sounds of the stadium have been enough.

Drug companies are quietly paying doctors and influencers to talk up their medicines online — and most people never see the full picture.
A 2024 study looked at doctors who posted about specific drugs or devices on X. Nearly all of them (93%) had taken money from the company that makes the product. Those payments added up to hundreds of thousands of dollars. The average doctor in the group received about $27,000 from the manufacturer. Most of the money came for speaking or consulting. Many of the posts were paid promotions, and some doctors never clearly said they were paid.
The numbers are even bigger for popular weight-loss drugs. One investigation found that two major companies paid more than 250,000 doctors and other prescribers over several years. The total spending topped $270 million. Some individual doctors received close to a million dollars. Companies say these payments help share science. Critics say the money can shape what doctors tell patients.
It is not only doctors. Celebrities and lifestyle influencers also get paid. In past cases the FDA sent warning letters after stars promoted drugs without mentioning risks. One famous example involved a well-known influencer and a morning-sickness pill. Similar problems have appeared with other paid posts.
A 2025 study of hundreds of popular social-media posts about common drugs found that 80% looked like unpaid promotions but carried signs of marketing. Only a tiny fraction used clear tags such as “#ad.” Drug companies themselves posted very few of them. Many posts talked about benefits but skipped serious side effects.
Patients see this content and ask their doctors about the drugs. In one survey, most doctors said patients had requested a medicine they first saw online, and many then wrote the prescription. Rules require companies to show both benefits and risks and to disclose payments, but enforcement has not kept up with the volume of posts.
The result is a system where money flows to the people patients trust most, yet the full story of those payments and the risks is often missing.

hits.text:
What if the same advice doctors give to protect your heart—eat less fat and lower your cholesterol—might quietly raise the risk of violence behind bars?
A surprising body of research has found that people with lower cholesterol levels are more likely to act aggressively or commit violent crimes. In one large Swedish study of nearly 80,000 adults, those with cholesterol below the median were roughly twice as likely to later be arrested for violent offenses, even after accounting for age, education, and alcohol use. Similar patterns appear in other groups: Indian men with violent criminal records had lower total and LDL cholesterol than non-offenders, and forensic psychiatric patients with lower cholesterol spent more time in seclusion for violent incidents.
Scientists think the link may involve brain chemistry. Cholesterol helps cell membranes work properly. When levels drop, serotonin signaling can weaken. Lower serotonin is a well-known factor in impulsivity and aggression. Experiments with monkeys support this idea—those put on low-fat, low-cholesterol diets became more aggressive and less social than monkeys on higher-fat diets.
Prison studies add another layer. In a landmark UK trial with young adult inmates, giving daily vitamin, mineral, and essential fatty acid supplements cut disciplinary offenses by about 26% overall and serious violent incidents by 37%, compared with placebo. Similar nutrient trials in other prisons have produced average drops in violence around 30%. Prison diets are often low in quality fats and key nutrients, which may compound the problem.
These findings do not prove that low cholesterol directly causes violence, and high cholesterol still raises heart-disease risk. They do suggest that aggressively lowering cholesterol—or feeding nutrient-poor diets—could have behavioral side effects worth considering, especially in populations already at higher risk for aggression. The evidence points to a possible trade-off: what’s good for arteries may not always be good for impulse control.

hits.name: Benjamin Bikman
hits.text:
One of the more ironic (though not really surprising) findings in obesity research is that carrying extra weight may help a person lose weight.

In one trial, adults with obesity wore either a heavy vest (11% of their body weight) or a light one (1%) for 8 hours a day for three weeks. The heavy-vest group lost more weight, and the difference was all fat (about 1.7 kg).

The obvious reason is that carrying more weight takes more energy, so every step costs a little more. Some researchers think there's more to it, and that the body may detect the extra load and respond by shedding some of its own fat to compensate.

Regardless of the mechanism, the evidence is clear: sometimes the way to get lighter is to make yourself heavier.
